questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft that has orbited the Moon.

answers.note: Columbia stayed in lunar orbit in July 1969 while Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the surface.
In December 1968 its crew became the first humans to orbit the Moon.
It has mapped the Moon from polar orbit since 2009 and photographed the Apollo landing sites.
Its crew flew the lunar module to within about 15 km of the surface in May 1969 as a full rehearsal.
The twin spacecraft mapped the Moon's gravity field in 2012 before a planned impact on the surface.
This 1998-99 polar orbiter found hydrogen enrichments at the lunar poles and was deliberately crashed into a south-pole crater.
NASA's 2013-14 orbiter sampled the Moon's thin exosphere and dust before impacting the far side.
Two retired THEMIS satellites were moved into lunar orbit in 2011 to study the Moon's space environment.
A small cubesat that entered a near-rectilinear halo orbit in November 2022 to test the path Gateway will use.
Apollo 15 and 16 each released a tiny satellite into lunar orbit to measure lunar gravity and magnetic fields.

questions.reveal: Cislunar space is the region every Apollo crew crossed on the way to the Moon, and a handful of small spacecraft still circle it today.

questions.prompt: Name something NASA left behind on the Moon.

answers.note: Eagle's lower half stayed at Tranquility Base when the crew lifted off in July 1969.
Apollo 15, 16 and 17 each left a battery-powered rover parked near the landing site.
Six Apollo crews planted US flags, and LRO imagery shows shadows from several of the flagpoles.
Apollo 12 and 14-17 deployed nuclear-powered geophysical stations that NASA switched off in 1977.
Apollo 11, 14 and 15 left passive mirrors that astronomers still use to measure the Earth-Moon distance.
Apollo 12 landed nearby in 1969 and its crew brought pieces of the 1967 robot lander home.
Apollo 13 through 17 steered their spent Saturn V third stages into the Moon to calibrate seismometers.
Several Apollo ascent stages were cast off after the crews rejoined the command module and later struck the Moon.

questions.reveal: With no atmosphere, wind or liquid water, nothing on the Moon rusts or blows away - only micrometeorites slowly erode it over millions of years.

questions.prompt: Name an instrument NASA left working on the Moon.

answers.note: Three Apollo arrays still return laser pulses fired from Earth, needing no electricity of their own.
ALSEP seismometers recorded moonquakes and meteorite impacts for years and revealed the Moon's internal structure.
These plutonium-238 power units ran the Apollo 12 and 14-17 experiment stations long after the crews left.
Several Apollo ALSEP stations carried magnetometers that measured the Moon's weak crustal magnetic field.
Apollo 15 and 17 placed thermometers in drilled holes to measure heat escaping from the lunar interior.
Apollo 12, 14 and 15 used this gauge to measure the Moon's extremely thin atmosphere.
Apollo 17's gravimeter was built to detect gravitational waves but was miscalibrated and returned no useful data.
Apollo 17's LEAM counted tiny meteorite impacts but overheated in the lunar daytime.

questions.reveal: The nuclear-powered ALSEP network ran until NASA shut it down on 30 September 1977, while the passive reflectors need no power at all.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft left in orbit around the Sun after its mission ended.

answers.note: Retired in October 2018 in a safe Earth-trailing solar orbit after confirming more than 2,600 exoplanets.
After three Mercury flybys in 1974-75 it was switched off and left circling the Sun.
This ion-propulsion technology demonstrator was retired in 2001 in solar orbit after imaging comet Borrelly.
In March 1959 it became the first US spacecraft to escape Earth's gravity, entering orbit around the Sun.
This ESA-NASA probe used a Jupiter gravity assist in 1992 to orbit over the Sun's poles until 2009.
The solar observatory lost contact in 2014 and NASA ended recovery efforts in 2018, leaving it in heliocentric orbit.
Repurposed to fly through comet Giacobini-Zinner's tail in 1985, it was later left in solar orbit with contact lost.
The 1976 NASA-German solar probe held the closest solar approach and fastest-spacecraft records until Parker Solar Probe.

questions.reveal: A heliocentric orbit has no drag to brake it, so a retired spacecraft like Kepler will keep circling the Sun indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA rover or lander that sits on the surface of Mars.

answers.note: It drove more than 45 km from 2004 until the 2018 global dust storm ended the mission.
Opportunity's twin worked in Gusev Crater for six years from 2004.
The nuclear-powered rover has climbed Mount Sharp in Gale Crater since landing in 2012.
It has been caching sealed rock samples in Jezero Crater since 2021.
The 1997 Pathfinder microrover was the first wheeled vehicle to drive on another planet.
This stationary lander recorded marsquakes from 2018 until accumulated dust ended it in 2022.
It dug into and confirmed water ice in the arctic plains in 2008.
The first successful US Mars landing, in 1976, operated for more than six years.
It touched down at Utopia Planitia in 1976 and returned data until 1980.

questions.reveal: Mars has no rain to rinse solar panels, so dust accumulation is what eventually silenced both InSight and Opportunity.

questions.prompt: Name a place on Mars where NASA has landed a spacecraft.

answers.note: Curiosity landed here in 2012 to study layered rocks recording an ancient lake.
Perseverance landed in 2021 at an ancient river delta to look for signs of past microbial life.
Opportunity found hematite blueberries here in 2004, mineral spheres that form in water.
Spirit explored this crater's floor and hills from 2004 until 2010.

Viking 1 touched down on the western slope of Chryse Planitia in 1976.

Phoenix landed in this northern arctic plain in 2008 and scraped exposed water ice.

questions.reveal: Landing sites are picked for science and safety - Jezero for its ancient river delta, Elysium Planitia for flat ground to place a seismometer.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft that has visited Jupiter.

answers.note: Its 1979 flyby revealed active volcanoes on Io and a faint ring around Jupiter.
It passed Jupiter in 1979 on the way to Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Juno entered a polar orbit in 2016 to map Jupiter's gravity and magnetic field beneath the clouds.
It orbited Jupiter from 1995 to 2003 and dropped a probe into the atmosphere.
In 1973 it became the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter.
Its 1974 Jupiter swingby used the planet's gravity to aim it toward Saturn.
It used a Jupiter gravity assist in 2007 to speed up on its way to Pluto.
Launched in October 2024, it is cruising toward Jupiter to survey Europa's ice shell and ocean.
The ESA-NASA probe used a Jupiter flyby in 1992 to tip into an orbit over the Sun's poles.

questions.reveal: Galileo was deliberately flown into Jupiter's atmosphere in 2003 so it could never crash into and contaminate Europa's possible ocean.

questions.prompt: Name a moon of Saturn that NASA's Cassini mission studied up close.

answers.note: Cassini mapped methane seas and rivers, and delivered ESA's Huygens probe to the surface in 2005.
Cassini discovered water-ice plumes erupting from a global subsurface ocean.
Its enormous Herschel impact crater gives this small moon a famously recognisable silhouette.
Cassini imaged its stark two-toned surface and a mountain ridge running along the equator.
Its wispy terrain turned out to be bright ice cliffs created by tectonic fractures.
Cassini searched around Saturn's second-largest moon for a faint ring system but found none.
The giant Odysseus impact basin and the Ithaca Chasma canyon dominate its surface.
Cassini imaged this irregular, sponge-textured moon, which tumbles unpredictably as it orbits.
Cassini photographed this distant irregular moon on arrival in 2004; it is likely a captured outer-solar-system body.

questions.reveal: Cassini was flown into Saturn's atmosphere on 15 September 2017 so it could never collide with Enceladus or Titan and contaminate them.

questions.prompt: Name a piece of NASA hardware that has crossed the heliopause.

answers.note: It crossed the heliopause on 25 August 2012, the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Each Voyager carries an identical gold-plated record of Earth's sounds, greetings and images.
Voyager 1's PWS measured the sharp rise in plasma density that confirmed it had left the heliosphere.
It recorded solar particles dropping away while galactic cosmic rays surged at the boundary.
The 3.7-metre dish still sends data home across a one-way light-time of more than 22 hours.
Three plutonium-238 generators per probe are slowly decaying, forcing NASA to switch instruments off.
It tracked how particles from the Sun fade away as the probes enter interstellar space.
Voyager's magnetometers measured the magnetic field of the interstellar medium beyond the heliopause.

questions.reveal: The heliopause is where the outward solar wind finally gives way to the pressure of interstellar gas, and both Voyagers still transmit from beyond it.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft that will never return to Earth.

answers.note: The most distant human-made object, it is moving away from the Sun at roughly 17 km every second.

The first probe to traverse the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter sent its last signal in 2003.

Pioneers 10 and 11 each carry a gold-anodised aluminium plaque depicting humans and a pulsar map.

questions.reveal: Beyond the heliopause there is nothing to slow these probes down, so they will keep drifting through the galaxy for billions of years.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA satellite left in Earth orbit when its mission ended.

answers.note: Launched on 17 March 1958, its solar-powered transmitter died in 1964 but it remains the oldest human-made object in orbit.

The Cosmic Background Explorer mapped the afterglow of the Big Bang from 1989 to 1993 and was then switched off in orbit.
NASA's first Tracking and Data Relay Satellite was retired in 2009 after more than 25 years and moved clear of the working fleet.
Three 1965 Saturn I launches unfolded huge wings to count micrometeoroid punctures, then were left in orbit when their batteries died.
A near-twin of LAGEOS-1, launched in 1992 with the Italian space agency and still laser-ranged from Earth today.

One of NASA's first communications satellites, launched in 1964 and switched off a few years later but still circling Earth.

questions.reveal: With almost no air at orbital altitude there is nothing to brake them - some of NASA's earliest satellites are still circling Earth decades after they fell silent.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA mission that studied Earth's radiation belts.

answers.note: The first US satellite, launched in 1958, carried James Van Allen's radiation detector - and discovered the belts by accident.

Purpose-built in 1958 to map the newly discovered belts with a suite of particle detectors.

Five 2007 probes timed the substorms that inject particles into the belts; two were later moved into lunar orbit as ARTEMIS.

questions.reveal: Explorer 1's detector kept saturating over the equator - NASA's very first satellite had stumbled on the radiation environment every crewed mission must cross.

questions.prompt: Name a piece of NASA launch hardware discarded on the way to orbit.

answers.note: The protective nose cone splits into halves and falls away once the rocket is above the thick part of the atmosphere.

The Saturn V's five-engine first stage burned for about two and a half minutes, then dropped away into the Atlantic.

Small solid rockets briefly fired to settle liquid propellant before an upper-stage restart, then were thrown away with the interstage.

questions.reveal: The first thing any mission abandons is the rocket that lifted it - most of a launch vehicle's mass never reaches space at all.

questions.prompt: Name a piece of hardware NASA discarded on the way to landing on Mars.

answers.note: The flat, solar-powered platform that flew the spacecraft from Earth was cut loose minutes before atmospheric entry.

questions.reveal: Almost every Mars landing throws away more hardware than it keeps - the cruise stage, aeroshell, parachute and descent gear are all gone within ten minutes.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft that has visited an asteroid.

questions.prompt: Name a piece of NASA hardware that has travelled beyond Neptune.

questions.prompt: Name a NASA spacecraft that has flown past a comet.
